data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: âChilling effectâ: US chips curb could slow down Asean data centre expansion, Malaysia and Thailand at higher risk, say analysts
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Washington’s new curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips could slow down the next phase of growth for South-east Asia’s data centre build-out, analysts said.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater risks from the restrictions due to their exposure to non-US data centre customers, while Singapore could see delays to its next wave of data centre development, they added.

The rule, issued by the US Department of Commerce on Monday (Nov 16), requires licences for advanced AI chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, with exemptions for US-headquartered companies.

The five countries account for about 7 to 9 per cent of the world’s operational data centre capacity at about 5.5 gigawatt (GW) of IT load, noted a DBS Group Research note released on Tuesday.

CGS International (CGSI) expects the ruling to benefit US hyperscalers, while DBS also noted that the rule could shift AI infrastructure investment “towards jurisdictions and operators facing fewer regulatory hurdles”.

“China-facing AI projects and independent graphics processing unit (GPU)-cloud operators face higher execution risks,” it noted in a report.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater exposure risk

Over in Malaysia, of the 8.4 GW of data centre power supply agreements signed with the government as at June, about 30 per cent is linked to US-headquartered companies.

The remaining users are “less clear”, noted the research house.

Meanwhile, colocation demand in Thailand data centres is also expected to slow down as the data centre operators that serve Chinese tech companies have to obtain US export licences when importing advanced AI chips from the US.

In Singapore, CGSI analysts said it believes the build-out for the second Data Centre Call for Application (DC-CFA2) and the upcoming data-centre park in Jurong Island “could be deferred”.

The research house cited “the potential souring of sentiments and demand”, following the new US rule as the primary reason for the slowdown.

In Singapore, four data centre operators – Digital Realty, Equinix, STT GDC and Keppel – were each provisionally allocated 50 megawatts (MW) under the DC-CFA2 tender in August.

Cristina Brayton-Lewis, partner at law firm White & Case, expects some “chilling effect” on data centre operators in Asean.

As a result of the new rule, some projects “may not be able to obtain necessary licences”, she said. “Other projects may be able to secure licences, but may face delays in licensing or potentially burdensome licensing conditions.”

Foo Zhiwei, analyst at Macquarie Capital, expects a “slowdown, not a halt”, as operators deal with the extra licensing requirements and additional know-your-customer checks.

DBS Group Research noted that the licensing requirements could delay GPU shipments and AI deployments.

The effects will be felt most among non-US cloud operators, noted DBS.

Operators still report strong demand

Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific at Digital Realty, said that the operator is still choosing tenants for its upcoming SIN13 data centre facility.

“We’re approached by so many people because we have the 50 MW, so we have to pick,” she said.

She added that the SIN13 data centre will host mostly AI inference and high-performance computing. Therefore, the company may lean towards companies that can more easily import GPUs under the new rules.

That said, she noted that the new rules means that the operator will “need to be more selective” of the customers it selects for the data centre.

Keppel, another of the four awarded capacity through the DC-CFA2, said it does not expect the measures to have a significant impact on its data centre business in Singapore.

“Most of our Singapore data centres, including the floating data centre under construction, are predominantly committed to US-based hyperscalers,” said a Keppel spokesperson.

Despite the restrictions, CGSI expects an upside for Singapore operators.

“(Singapore) could benefit over time if it establishes itself as a trusted computing hub for compliant workloads and hyperscalers,” the research house noted.

Chip suppliers at risk

While demand for operators remains strong, analysts warned that chip suppliers are at the biggest risk.

AEM is directly exposed through its AI and high-performance computing customers, while UMS, Frencken and Venture could be impacted indirectly, noted CGSI.

“We think the key risk to earnings is a slower and more measured demand pace from customers, which could potentially affect earnings growth pace over FY2027 and (potentially) FY2028,” noted the research house.

However, DBS said that the impact on equipment makers is limited.

“The measures primarily target advanced computing chips rather than equipment,” said DBS, noting that UMS and Frencken are less affected.

“While slower AI capacity expansion could eventually weigh on wafer fab equipment spending, UMS and Frencken are less affected in the near term.”

However, DBS noted that Venture might be affected, given its exposure to AI infrastructure hardware, networking and test equipments

Overall, CGSI expects investments to slow down mainly “as investors await licensing clarity”.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Tuesday said Singapore can facilitate US checks on companies and how advanced chips brought into the country are deployed, if Washington has concerns.

He noted that a large portion of chips recorded, as sales to Singapore never enter the country.

“Only a small volume of those chips’ directly comes into Singapore,” said PM Wong.

data.title: When AI systems are compromised, detection without recovery is not resilience
data.description:
RECENT data breaches involving MoneySmart, M1 and Doctor Anywhere have put cyber risks back in focus for Singapore businesses.

On Nov 13, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore urged all organisations to “take immediate steps to strengthen their cyberdefences”.

While most conversations have focused on how these incidents happened and what information was exposed, they raise a bigger, more urgent question for business leaders. If critical systems are hit, how long can the business afford to be out of action before the financial, operational and reputational damage begin to pile up?

Consider two incidents with very different outcomes.

In September 2026, Boustead Singapore disclosed that an overseas business unit had isolated affected systems, activated business continuity procedures and recovered critical data and systems from backups following a cyberincident. Its operations suffered no material disruption.

Contrast that with the 2025 cyberattack on Marks & Spencer, which forced systems offline and disrupted online operations for weeks.

While physical stores continued trading, customers could not access certain online shopping services, with operations returning in phases.

The circumstances were different, but both incidents highlight a key point. Getting systems back online is one thing; knowing whether the business can safely resume operations is another.

As organisations give artificial-intelligence agents access to sensitive systems, leaders must ask: Can the team determine what happened, contain the consequences and safely reverse unintended outcomes?

Commvault’s 2026 State of Data Resilience report found that only 45 per cent of organisations in Singapore are very confident that they could identify a compromised AI system.

If organisations are not even confident they can identify a compromised AI system, determining what has been affected, what needs to be recovered, and whether the team can restore it to a clean, trusted state could be even more challenging.

AI changes the nature of the blast radius

As AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf, the nature of operational risk changes.

An autonomous AI agent may make decisions and take actions across multiple connected systems using identities and permissions legitimately granted by the organisation.

This autonomy creates business value, but it also means that a compromised identity, inaccurate data, incomplete instruction or poorly designed workflow can trigger consequences across data, applications and business processes before a person has time to intervene.

The challenge then is to understand the chain of actions that followed.

What data did the system access? What decisions did it influence? Which transactions did it initiate? What downstream processes accepted its output? Which actions need to be reversed, reconciled or reviewed. Without that understanding, an organisation cannot know whether the incident is truly contained.

And if it cannot establish which data and systems remain trustworthy, restoring the affected technology may not be enough.

Recover what the business needs, then prove that it works

No organisation can restore everything at once. Recovery, therefore, needs to begin with understanding which capabilities the business needs first, and what those capabilities depend on.

The minimum viable company, or MVC, defines the systems, data and operations that must remain available, or be restored first, for the organisation to continue functioning during disruption.

An MVC differs by organisation. For a bank, it might include enabling customers to make time-critical payments and withdraw funds.

For a logistics provider, it might mean accepting shipping instructions, tracking goods in transit and releasing deliveries at their destination.

The priority is to determine which business processes must continue or be restored first, and then map the systems, data, people and other dependencies needed to support them.

The same principle applies to AI. One business process supported by AI may require rapid recovery, while another one may tolerate a longer interruption.

Prioritisation should therefore be based on business impact and recovery requirements, not simply on whether a workload uses AI.

It must also account for the identities, applications, infrastructure and data required to restore the complete business process safely.

Boards do not need to know every recovery dependency or direct the operational response.

But they should require evidence that management has identified the organisation’s critical business capabilities, and agreed on the order in which they will be restored cleanly and tested so that they can operate safely following disruption.

The next test for trusted AI: Recovery readiness

As Singapore advances trusted AI, resilience must become part of that trust. Guardrails matter, but so does knowing the business can recover when those are not enough.

As AI moves from assisting to acting, recovery readiness must become part of AI readiness.

Singapore businesses must be able to demonstrate that they can contain unintended consequences, restore critical operations and recover safely when existing safeguards fall short.

The writer is field chief technology officer for Asia-Pacific at Commvault

AI tools were used to support research, framework development and proofreading of the article before submission

data.title: STI opens 1.4% lower on Friday, tracking losses across Wall Street
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stocks were pulled into negative territory on Friday (Nov 20) morning, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street, where Anthropic’s much-anticipated Nasdaq debut failed to lift the broader market.

As at 9.30 am, the Straits Times Index (STI) opened 1.4 per cent or 68.48 points lower at 5,011.01. Across the broader market, losers outnumbered gainers 276 to 67 after 190 million securities worth S$345.4 million changed hands.

Most counters were down. Banking stocks were trading lower, with DBS shedding 1.5 per cent or S$0.99 to S$66.35. OCBC was down 2.5 per cent or S$0.69 at S$26.73. UOB fell 1.5 per cent or S$0.54 to S$35.60.

Among STI counters, offshore, marine and energy specialist Seatrium was the biggest decliner, which was trading 4.7 per cent or S$0.08 lower at S$1.63.

Tech stocks were in the negative territory as well. As at 9.36 am, AEM was down 7.9 per cent at S$5.80, UMS fell 6.4 per cent to S$1.62, CSE Global declined 5.2 per cent to S$0.73, Frencken was down 7.1 per cent at S$1.58, and Addvalue Tech dropped 3.9 per cent to S$0.098.

Gold mining stock CNMC was down 5.3 per cent at S$0.80. Gold hit its lowest level in more than a year on Wednesday before paring some losses on Thursday. Analysts had said weaker gold prices could squeeze CNMC’s mining margins, particularly if operating costs remained high.

Wall Street stocks ended lower on Thursday after Anthropic’s super-sized initial public offering failed to revitalise faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early spike in its share price ebbed.

Anthropic shares opened at US$111.50 apiece and quickly rose as high as US$115 a share, or 38.6 per cent above the offer price, but pared those gains to 17.1 per cent by the end of the session.

Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced late Wednesday at US$83 a share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade. The stock opened shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed US$2 trillion, its momentum began to lose steam.

data.title: Nvidia asked to sell chips to companies tied to Chinese military and Megaspeed
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday (Nov 19) showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon.

The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that The New York Times reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory.

The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO.

The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director.

The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said.

They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X.

The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems.

The committee cited reporting by The New York Times that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres.

Two reports from The New York Times first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal.

The New York Times reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed.

The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week. The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China.

The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China.

Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating.

The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said.

John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China.

Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said.

A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance.

A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said.

President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check.

Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms.

Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move.

In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”.

The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications.

Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said.

Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”.

“Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. NYTIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Mistral AI opens regional HQ in Singapore, seeks to fill 200 roles in Apac
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] French artificial intelligence firm Mistral AI opened its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore on Friday (Nov 19), to host most of the 200 staff that it plans to have in the region by 2027.

The company had around 40 staff in Singapore in May, when CEO Arthur Mensch told The Business Times that it was planning for 100 employees by the end of the year.

Geoff Soon, vice-president of revenue for the Asia-Pacific at Mistral, told BT that Singapore is “not a sales and marketing team”.

“I would say it is about 70 per cent forward deployment capabilities,” he said, pointing out that the company will hire a mix of forward deployment engineers and scientists to fill the Singapore headcount.

He added that Mistral will be looking to hire talents from “leading universities” for these roles.

Forward deployment – a term that has recently gathered pace due to the rise of AI – is the practice of allowing engineers to directly communicate with customers.

Soon said that unlike other tech firms, where engineers typically only fine-tune AI models, the individuals that Mistral recruits will be directly involved in development. “Scientists do the models, the engineers do the agentic capability,” he explained.

Talent is one of the reasons why the company set up its regional headquarters in Singapore. Soon noted that the Republic has hosted several multinational manufacturing firms for a long period, giving Mistral an existing talent pool to draw from.

However, he acknowledged that the company will also need to tap people from outside Singapore for roles that workers here cannot fill.

The company will therefore seek to hire an even split of local and international talents. Soon noted that, to this end, Singapore “offers an amazing culture”, which will make it easier to convince people to relocate here.

Targeting regulated industries

Mistral develops open-source and open-weight large language models. This means that the AI models can run locally on-premises, within company servers, allowing for greater sovereignty and security.

Soon said that the company will, building on its strengths, focus on serving regulated industries such as financial services and the public sector.

Mistral already has a presence in Singapore through partnerships with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, as well as DSO National Laboratories. The company also has “other customers that are very focused on creating custom models to deliver their sovereign capabilities”.

Asked about his biggest concern about Mistral’s expansion plans, Soon said that more investments need to be made in the digital infrastructure layer. This includes access to more compute such as data centres and chips.

“We need lots of infrastructure,” he added, “to run our experiments and to develop new capabilities as we start to move into longer running agents.”

data.title: S-Reitsâ game plan: Sell non-core assets and redevelop properties
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-Reits) are stepping up efforts to recycle capital through divestments to improve their portfolio returns, said industry observers.

Credit rating agency Fitch Ratings expects S-Reits to focus on selling non-core properties and redeveloping existing assets to refresh their portfolios.

The agency also expects acquisitions to be opportunistic, with trusts recycling capital into yield-accretive investments to enhance portfolio quality and returns, it said on Wednesday (Nov 18).

S-Reits rated by Fitch sold about S$1.1 billion worth of non-core properties in the 12 months to end-September, compared with about S$850 million in acquisitions.

Deal activity was led by Frasers Logistics and Commercial Trust, ESR Reit, CapitaLand Ascott Trust (Clas) and Stoneweg Reit.

Capital recycling is also gathering pace, Jefferies analysts Geraldine Wong and Wilson Ng said in a report published on Nov 11.

They said: “Several Reits are accelerating divestments and portfolio repositioning, particularly of slower-growth overseas assets. We see this as another potential distribution per unit (DPU) growth lever, providing capacity to redeploy capital into higher-return opportunities.”

For instance, Clas completed the S$360 million sale of The Robertson House on Jul 30. It used part of the proceeds to acquire Coliwoo Midtown, a 212-room co-living property at 141 Middle Road, for S$134 million on Sep 30.

Clas’ manager said Coliwoo Midtown’s pro forma earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) yield of 4.1 per cent was 1.8 percentage points higher than the hotel’s exit yield of 2.3 per cent.

Meanwhile, ESR Reit completed S$472.4 million worth of non-core asset sales in the first nine months of 2026.

These included the S$101 million sale of a hotel strata lot at ESR BizPark @ Changi, 46A Tanjong Penjuru for S$113.5 million and 12 Ang Mo Kio Street 65 for S$33.3 million.

Fitch said: “We expect non-core asset sales to remain an important source of funding for portfolio rejuvenation and balance-sheet management.”

It pointed to Mapletree Industrial Trust’s (MIT) plan to sell about S$500 million to S$600 million worth of North American assets, prioritising data centres that are vacant or due to become vacant.

In August, MIT put a portfolio of 22 older US data centres for sale, valued at about US$1.24 billion in aggregate, with US$1.07 billion attributable to the trust.

At its October results briefing, the manager said it aimed to complete a “good amount” of the disposals by the end of FY2027.

Data centres account for about 57 per cent, or S$4.7 billion, of MIT’s S$8.3 billion portfolio.

Jefferies’ Wong and Ng said: “Pruning its underperforming US data centre portfolio better positions MIT for longer-term growth. Nearer term, channelling divestment proceeds to pay down higher-cost US-dollar debt could even be DPU-accretive, albeit slightly NAV-dilutive if sold below book values.”

While MIT’s strategy of divesting older US assets and redeploying capital into modern data centres in Japan and Europe is positive, Wong and Ng said its execution would take time.

“We would wait for clearer signs of stabilisation before turning positive,” they added.

Jefferies had a “hold” call on MIT, with a lower target price of S$1.85. Fitch rated the trust BBB+ with a stable outlook.

Development and asset enhancement to become ‘more important’

Fitch added that development and asset enhancement initiatives will become “more important” for some issuers seeking to improve portfolio quality and asset returns.

Given the significant differences in leverage headroom among the S-Reits rated by Fitch, the agency expects trusts with stronger balance sheets to have greater flexibility to pursue acquisitions when opportunities arise.

Fitch expects MIT and Starhill Global Reit to retain wide rating headroom as they use divestment proceeds to pare debt.

By contrast, the agency expects redevelopment to keep leverage elevated at ESR Reit and CapitaLand India Trust.

Their Ebitda net leverage should remain manageable, Fitch said, assuming they fund construction with debt alongside equity or divestment proceeds.

data.title: Citi incorrectly booked trades, underestimated risky assets by US$35 billion, sources say
data.description:
CITIGROUP incorrectly booked trades at a European subsidiary that underestimated its risk-weighted assets, two people familiar with the matter said, in a setback for the US lender that has been trying to fix regulatory issues.

Citigroup underestimated risk-weighted assets by about US$35 billion at a trading unit in Europe, one person familiar with the matter said.

In a statement to Reuters, Citigroup said the bank had identified and resolved an internal capital modelling issue at a European trading subsidiary this summer.

“The subsidiary remained fully compliant with regulatory minimums throughout, with no impact on the holding company or main operating bank,” the bank said. “Citi completed remedial actions and injected capital to immediately restore the subsidiary’s buffers.”

The Wall Street firm incorrectly recorded trades at its UK securities unit using an internal model based on its own statistical assumptions, the people said. Regulators had not approved the model for those types of transactions, they added.

Once the trades were recorded using a standard risk model, the value of risk-weighted assets shot up significantly, the people said.

The mishap is a setback for Citi CEO Jane Fraser, who has been trying to get the bank out of the regulatory penalty box for years.

Citi has operated under tight supervisory scrutiny and as recently as the summer was targeting submitting paperwork to regulators this year to get the restrictions lifted, Reuters has reported.

Shaking off the regulatory shackles would free up resources, become a key achievement for Fraser and bolster Citigroup shares, according to analysts.

Citi’s problems stretch back to 2020, when it was told to remediate longstanding risk management and data governance problems identified by the US Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

It was fined US$400 million and agreed to a long list of longstanding issues it needed to fix, but was then fined another US$136 million in 2024 for the delay in fixing its data management problems. REUTERS
